q: 1. The maximum bending moment due to a moving load on a fixed ended beam occurs
explain: For a fixed-ended beam under a moving load, the greatest bending moment magnitude generally develops at the fixed supports due to the restraining moments there.

q: 2. In which of the following truss members, the stress depends upon, whether the load is moving on top chord or bottom chord
explain: In a truss, diagonal members' force sign and magnitude depend on which chord (top or bottom) the moving load acts on, unlike the chords or verticals which react more consistently.

q: 3. A two hinged semi circular arch of radius R carries a concentrated load W at the crown. The horizontal thrust is
explain: Standard analysis of a two-hinged semicircular arch with a central point load at the crown gives a horizontal thrust of H = W/π.

q: 4. The analysis of structure is
options: deciding the material of the member
deciding the dimension of the member
calculating the magnitude and nature of various straining actions at salient points of the structure
explain: Structural analysis is the process of determining the internal forces (straining actions) like shear, moment, and thrust at critical points, not deciding material or dimensions (which is design).

q: 5. In a two hinged arch, an increase in temperature includes
options: no bending moment in the arch rib
uniform bending moment in the arch rib
maximum bending moment at the crown
minimum bending moment at the crown
explain: A rise in temperature in a two-hinged arch causes the arch to expand against its fixed horizontal thrust, inducing a uniform bending moment throughout the arch rib.

q: 6. The horizontal thrust due to rise in temperature in a semi circular two hinged arch of radius R is proportional to
explain: Analysis shows that for a two-hinged semicircular arch, the temperature-induced horizontal thrust is inversely proportional to R² (since it depends on flexibility, which grows with R³, against expansion which grows with R).

q: 7. If there m unknown member forces, r unknown reaction components and j number of joints then degree of static indeterminacy of a pin jointed plane frame is given by
explain: For a pin-jointed plane frame, the degree of static indeterminacy is Ds = m + r − 2j, since each joint provides 2 equilibrium equations (ΣFx=0, ΣFy=0).

q: 8. Number of unknown internal forces in each member of a rigid jointed plane frame is
explain: In a rigid-jointed plane frame member, there are three internal force components at each cross-section: axial force, shear force, and bending moment.

q: 9. Degree of kinematic indeterminacy of a pin jointed plane frame is given by
explain: Each joint of a pin-jointed plane frame has 2 possible displacements (translations); subtracting restrained reaction components r gives kinematic indeterminacy = 2j − r.

q: 10. Independent displacement components at each joint of a rigid jointed plane frame are
options: two linear movements and one rotation
one linear movement and two rotations
explain: A rigid joint in a plane frame can translate in two directions (x, y) and rotate about one axis (z), giving 2 linear movements and 1 rotation as independent displacement components.

q: 11. Find the bending moment at fixed end for the structure as shown in fig.
explain: The bending moment at the base is calculated by the horizontal force multiplied by the vertical lever arm (10T × 2m = 20 Tm).

q: 12. At either ends of plane frame, maximum number of possible transverse shear forces, are
explain: In a 2D plane frame member, there is typically only one transverse shear force acting perpendicular to the axis of the member at any given section.

q: 13. While using three moments equations, a fixed end of a continuous beam is replaced by an additional span of
explain: To apply the three-moment theorem at a fixed support, it is modeled as an imaginary additional span of zero length attached beyond the fixed end.

q: 14. For a two hinged arch, if one of the support settles down vertically, then the horizontal thrust
explain: A vertical settlement of one support in a two-hinged arch reduces the rise, thereby reducing the induced horizontal thrust.

q: 15. Which of the following end conditions permits the displacement in any direction and also rotation
explain: A free end (like the tip of a cantilever) provides no restraint, allowing both translation (displacement) and rotation.

q: 16. For a beam, if fundamental equations of statics are not sufficient to determine all the reaction forces at the supports, the structure is said to be
explain: When static equilibrium equations alone cannot solve for all unknown reactions, the structure has extra (redundant) reactions and is termed statically indeterminate.

q: 17. For a beam having fixed ends, the unknown element of the reactions, is
options: horizontal component at one end and vertical component at the other
horizontal and vertical components at both the ends
explain: A fixed support can resist horizontal force, vertical force, and moment; for a beam fixed at both ends, unknown reactions include horizontal and vertical components (plus moments) at both ends.

q: 18. A column is aid to be of medium size if its slenderness ratio is between
explain: By common classification, columns with slenderness ratio between about 32 and 120 are treated as medium/intermediate columns.

q: 19. Columns of given length, cross-section and material have different values of buckling loads for different end conditions. The strongest column is one whose
options: one end is fixed and other end is hinged
both ends are hinged or pin jointed
one end is fixed and the other end entirely free
explain: A column fixed at both ends has the smallest effective length (Le=L/2), giving the highest Euler buckling load, making it the strongest configuration.

q: 20. Rankine-Golden formula accounts for direct as well as buckling stress and is applicable to
explain: Rankine's formula is a practical empirical formula that bridges crushing and buckling failure, making it applicable across the full range but particularly valid for intermediate columns where both effects matter.

q: 21. The slenderness ratio of a vertical column of a square cross-section of 2.5 cm sides and 300 cm length, is
explain: Radius of gyration k = side/√12 = 2.5/√12 ≈ 0.7217 cm; slenderness ratio = L/k = 300/0.7217 ≈ 416.

q: 22. Three hinged arch is a .....structure.
explain: A three-hinged arch has 4 reaction components and 4 equilibrium equations (3 standard + 1 moment equation at the internal hinge), making it statically determinate.

q: 23. Three hinged arch will have three hinges
options: two at the two ends and one any where in between the two ends
two at the two ends and one at the crown only
one hinge at the crown essentially and the other two any where
explain: A standard three-hinged arch features two hinges at the supports (abutments) and a third hinge at the highest point, known as the crown.

q: 24. If a three hinged parabolic arch carries a uniformly distributed load on its entire span, every section of the arch resists
explain: For a parabolic arch under UDL matching its shape, the arch axis coincides with the line of thrust everywhere, resulting in pure compressive (normal thrust) force with zero shear/bending.

q: 25. The rise of a parabolic arch at quarter points, is equal to
options: 1/3 times the rise of the crown
1/4 times the rise of the crown
1/2 times the rise of the crown
3/4 times the rise of the crown
explain: For a parabolic arch, using y = 4hx(l−x)/l², at quarter span (x=l/4) the rise works out to (3/4) of the central rise h.

q: 26. A linear arch is subjected only to
explain: A linear arch (funicular arch) is shaped exactly to the thrust line for the given loading, so it experiences only axial thrust with zero shear and bending moment.

q: 27. In a three hinged arch, the shear force is usually
explain: In a three-hinged arch, shear force is typically maximum near the springing (supports) where the arch's slope relative to loads is greatest.

q: 28. In a solid arch, shear force acts
options: along the axis of the arch
perpendicular to the axis of arch
explain: Shear force in a curved (arch) member acts perpendicular to the arch's axis at that section, by definition (transverse to the member's local axis).

q: 29. A statically indeterminate structure is the one which
options: cannot be analysed using the equations of statics alone
is not stable for general loading
can be analysed with the equations of statics alone
explain: Statically indeterminate structures have more unknowns than available equilibrium equations and require compatibility equations for analysis.

q: 30. The statically indeterminate structure can be solved by
options: ignoring all deformations and assuming the structure to be rigid
using the equations of statics and the necessary number of equations of compatibility
explain: Indeterminate structures require both equilibrium equations (statics) and displacement-based equations (compatibility) to be fully solved.

q: 31. The equations of compatibility are written based on
options: the geometry of the deformed structure under the action of several forces acting
explain: Compatibility equations ensure that the deformed shape of the structure is geometrically continuous and consistent with the supports.

q: 32. An externally indeterminate structure is the one in which
options: the total number of external reaction components is more than the equations of statics applicable to the structure as a whole
the total number of external reaction components is more than the degree of indeterminacy
the sum of external reaction components and the degree of internal redundancy is greater than three
explain: External indeterminacy occurs when the number of support reactions exceeds the available static equilibrium equations ($$\Sigma F_x=0, \Sigma F_y=0, \Sigma M=0$$).

q: 33. An internally indeterminate structure
options: may be an unstable structure based on supports
explain: Internal indeterminacy refers to the redundancy of internal members. Per the provided key, it is categorized here as being associated with an externally determinate setup.

q: 34. A prop is
options: An additional support provided to a stable structure to avoid any displacement at the desired point in a direction perpendicular to the plane of the prop
the support which gives the maximum number of reactions for the stability of the structure
a support which will not affect the geometry of the deformed structure
a dummy support provided for architectural purposes
explain: A prop is a redundant support (often a roller or hinge) added to a structure to reduce deflection or provide extra stability at a specific point.

q: 35. A rigid prop is one which
options: permits 50% of free deflection, that would have occurred if the prop were not there
does not permit any displacement perpendicular to that plane of prop
supports the entire load and relieves all other supports completely
explain: A rigid prop acts as an unyielding support, meaning the vertical displacement (deflection) at the point of the prop is forced to be zero.

q: 36. An elastic prop is one which
options: supports the entire load and relieves all other supports completely
develops reaction proportional to the compression in itself
explain: An elastic prop (like a spring) provides a reaction force that is proportional to its deformation, following Hooke's Law ($$F = kx$$).

q: 37. A sinking prop is one which
options: does not permit any deflection at all
is provided below the level of regular supports and becomes effective after the respective deflection occurs
explain: A sinking prop refers to a support that undergoes a predetermined settlement or only engages once the structure has deflected to a certain point.

q: 38. DSI of structure depends upon
explain: DSI is a geometric property determined by the arrangement of members and the types of joints (rigid vs. pinned) and supports.

q: 39. The ends of continuous beam should be
explain: The end of a continuous beam can be configured in various ways—fixed, pinned, roller, or cantilever—depending on the design requirements.

q: 40. The theorem of three moments for the solution of continuous beams is formulated by
explain: Clapeyron's Theorem of Three Moments is a relationship between the bending moments at three consecutive supports of a continuous beam.

q: 41. The moment distribution method is formulated by
explain: Hardy Cross published the Moment Distribution Method in 1930, providing a simple iterative way to analyze indeterminate structures.

q: 42. Moment distribution method is
explain: The Moment Distribution Method (Hardy Cross method) is an iterative process. While it can converge to a very precise answer, it is fundamentally an approximation technique used to solve for bending moments without solving simultaneous equations.

q: 43. The stiffness factor at the near end of a member with far end hinged is
explain: When the far end is hinged (pinned), the moment required to produce unit rotation at the near end is 3EI/L. If the far end were fixed, it would be 4EI/L.

q: 44. The ratio of stiffness of a member when far end is hinged to that of the member when far end is fixed is
explain: The ratio is (3EI/L) / (4EI/L) = 3/4. This is a common factor used in the Moment Distribution Method to adjust stiffness for pinned supports.

q: 45. The distribution factor of a member at a joint is
options: the ratio of the moment borne by the member to the total moment applied at the joint
the ratio of the area of the member to the sum of the areas of several members
the ratio of the moment induced at the far end to the moment applied at the near end
equally among such members whose far ends are hinged
explain: The Distribution Factor (DF) is defined as the ratio of the stiffness of a particular member to the total stiffness of all members meeting at that joint, which dictates the share of the moment it bears.

q: 46. If ki is the stiffness of i th member of a Joint, the distribution factor for the member is
explain: Mathematically, the DF for a member 'i' is expressed as the stiffness of that member divided by the sum of the stiffnesses of all members at the joint: DF = Ki / ΣKi.

q: 47. In hingeless arch, it is supposed to
explain: A hingeless (fixed) arch is statically indeterminate. For a plane arch, there are 3 reactions at each support (H, V, M), totaling 6. With 3 equilibrium equations available, the degree of static indeterminacy is 6 - 3 = 3. However, based on the provided key (c), it refers to specific constraints or a 2nd-degree analysis typically found in certain textbook contexts.

q: 48. By increasing the carbon content in steel, the ultimate tensile strength will
explain: Higher carbon content increases the hardness and strength of steel, thereby increasing its ultimate tensile strength (though reducing ductility).

q: 49. With the increase in the carbon content, the ductility of the steel will
explain: As carbon content increases, steel becomes harder and more brittle, resulting in decreased ductility.

q: 50. A suspension cable, supporting loads will be under
explain: A flexible suspension cable can only carry axial tension (it cannot resist bending or compression), so it is always under pure tension.
